question: Why do magnetic bacteria in northern ponds swim towards magnetic north?
answer: To go down. A chain of magnetite crystals inside each cell works as a compass needle, and in the northern hemisphere field lines dip into the ground, so swimming north along them leads into the low-oxygen mud they need. Southern strains swim south; at the magnetic equator, where lines lie flat, both kinds turn up.
move: Ask what a navigator is trying to reach, not just which way it points.
reference: Blakemore, Frankel & Kalmijn, South-seeking magnetotactic bacteria in the Southern Hemisphere, Nature, 1980
